reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Results from impaired lymphatic drainage causing accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid and progressive limb swelling
Primary forms arise from congenital or inherited lymphatic maldevelopment, while secondary forms follow damage from surgery, radiotherapy, malignancy, infection, or trauma
Worldwide, filarial infection is the leading cause of secondary lymphoedema, whereas in high-income settings cancer treatment predominates
Early swelling is soft and pitting but becomes non-pitting and fibrotic over time, with skin thickening and a positive Stemmer sign at the base of the toes
The distribution characteristically includes the dorsum of the foot and toes, helping distinguish it from other causes of limb swelling
Diagnosis is largely clinical; lymphoscintigraphy can confirm lymphatic dysfunction when the cause is uncertain
Cornerstone management is complete decongestive therapy with skin care, manual lymphatic drainage, compression, and exercise
Meticulous skin hygiene reduces recurrent cellulitis, which itself further damages lymphatics and worsens the oedema
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphoedema develops when lymphatic transport capacity is exceeded by the lymphatic load, leading to accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitium. In primary disease the lymphatic vessels or nodes are congenitally hypoplastic, aplastic, or dysfunctional. In secondary disease, previously normal lymphatics are obstructed or destroyed by surgery, radiotherapy, tumour infiltration, recurrent infection (notably filariasis), or trauma. Stagnant protein draws further fluid osmotically and incites chronic inflammation, fibrosis, adipose deposition, and skin changes, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Impaired local immune surveillance predisposes to recurrent cellulitis.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic venous insufficiency and venous oedema
Systemic causes of oedema (cardiac, renal, hepatic, hypoalbuminaemia)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment including Stemmer sign and limb circumference or volume measurement
Lymphoscintigraphy to confirm lymphatic dysfunction when the diagnosis is unclear
Duplex ultrasound to exclude venous disease or thrombosis
Cross-sectional imaging to identify malignancy or nodal obstruction in secondary cases
Evaluation for filariasis in endemic regions
redFlags: Features of cellulitis (spreading erythema, warmth, fever) requiring prompt treatment
Rapidly progressive or unilateral swelling raising concern for underlying malignancy
New or changing cutaneous lesions suggesting lymphangiosarcoma in longstanding lymphoedema
Sudden painful swelling that could indicate concurrent deep vein thrombosis
reference.prognosis: Lymphoedema is generally a chronic, progressive condition without cure, but sustained decongestive therapy and compression can control swelling, preserve function, and reduce complications. Poor adherence, recurrent infection, and untreated underlying causes worsen the outlook, and rarely longstanding disease can undergo malignant change.
pitfalls: Confusing lymphoedema with venous oedema or lipoedema and applying inappropriate treatment
Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial disease
Overlooking an underlying malignancy in new unilateral limb swelling
Neglecting skin care, allowing recurrent cellulitis that accelerates progression
management: Complex decongestive therapy with manual lymphatic drainage, multilayer compression bandaging transitioning to fitted compression garments, and remedial exercise
Meticulous skin and nail care with emollients to protect the barrier and reduce infection
Prompt antibiotics for cellulitis, with antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent attacks
Treat the underlying cause, such as antifilarial therapy with diethylcarbamazine in filariasis or relieving nodal obstruction in malignancy
Weight management and limb elevation as adjuncts to compression
Surgical options such as lymphaticovenous anastomosis, vascularised lymph-node transfer, or liposuction and debulking for refractory or advanced disease
Monitor limb volume and remain alert to the rare cutaneous angiosarcoma complicating longstanding lymphoedema
